```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r}
library(robotcompR)
```

A path is a geometric curve; a trajectory adds timing. robotcompR returns
trajectories as `robot_trajectory` objects with sampled `time`, `q`, `qd`
and `qdd`, and (for analytic profiles) an `evaluate()` closure for exact
values at any time.

## Polynomial point to point motion

A quintic matches position, velocity and acceleration at both ends. With zero
boundary velocity and acceleration, the normalized profile is the familiar
$s(\tau) = 10\tau^3 - 15\tau^4 + 6\tau^5$.

```{r}
tr <- robot_traj_polynomial(q0 = c(0, 1), q1 = c(1, -1), duration = 2,
                            qd0 = c(0.5, 0), qd1 = c(0, 0.3))
tr
e <- tr$evaluate(c(0, 2))
e$q
e$qd
plot(tr, "q")
plot(tr, "qd")
```

The cubic option matches only position and velocity, so its acceleration
jumps at the endpoints. Outside $[0, T]$ the trajectory is held at rest at
its endpoint positions.

Without a robot, the joint order comes from the names of `q0`. Named
endpoints with the same names are matched by name:

```{r}
named <- robot_traj_polynomial(c(a = 0, b = 1), c(b = 3, a = 2), duration = 1, n = 3)
named$q
```

## Trapezoidal velocity profiles

`robot_traj_trapezoidal()` accelerates at `amax`, cruises at `vmax` and
decelerates. All joints share one time scaling, so joint space motion is a
straight line and the slowest joint sets the duration:

$$
T = \frac{\Delta}{v_{\max}} + \frac{v_{\max}}{a_{\max}}
\quad\text{when}\quad \Delta \ge \frac{v_{\max}^2}{a_{\max}},
\qquad T = 2\sqrt{\Delta / a_{\max}} \quad\text{otherwise}.
$$

```{r}
tz <- robot_traj_trapezoidal(c(0, 0), c(1, 2), vmax = 1, amax = 2)
tz$duration
apply(abs(tz$qd), 2, max)
plot(tz, "qd")
```

## Multi-waypoint paths

`robot_traj_path()` times a polyline (for example a planner output) as a
sequence of rest to rest trapezoidal segments. This is conservative but
always respects the limits and never overshoots a waypoint.

```{r}
path <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(1, 0), c(1, 1), c(0.2, 1.4))
tp <- robot_traj_path(path, vmax = 1, amax = 2, dt = 0.01)
tp$duration
plot(tp$q[, 1], tp$q[, 2], type = "l", asp = 1, xlab = "q1", ylab = "q2")
points(path, pch = 19, col = "firebrick")
```

## Checking a trajectory against a robot

```{r}
arm <- robot_example("planar2")
robot_traj_check(arm, tp)$ok
bad <- robot_traj_polynomial(c(0, 0), c(4, 0), 1)
chk <- robot_traj_check(arm, bad)
chk$ok
head(chk$violations)
```

## Cartesian motion

`robot_traj_cartesian()` moves the end effector along a straight line with a
quintic time scaling $s(t)$, interpolating orientation by slerp,
$R(s) = \exp(s\,\hat\phi) R_0$ with $\phi = \log(R_1 R_0^\top)$. The spatial
velocity is $\dot s\,(p_1 - p_0, \phi)$ and the acceleration
$\ddot s\,(p_1 - p_0, \phi)$, returned as `velocity` and `acceleration`.
The conversion to joints can be done by hand, seeding each inverse kinematics
solve with the previous solution:

```{r}
from <- robot_pose(translation = c(1.5, 0.3, 0))
to <- robot_pose(translation = c(0.8, 1.2, 0))
ct <- robot_traj_cartesian(from, to, duration = 2, n = 21)
q <- c(0.3, -0.8)
Q <- matrix(NA, length(ct$poses), 2)
for (i in seq_along(ct$poses)) {
  q <- robot_ik(arm, ct$poses[[i]], initial = q, weights = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0))$q
  Q[i, ] <- q
}
P <- robot_fk_positions(arm, Q)
plot(P[, 1], P[, 2], type = "b", asp = 1, xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "y (m)")
```

or by passing `robot`. The joint velocities and accelerations then describe
the joint path that is returned. Their task part solves $J\dot q = V$ and
$J\ddot q = A - \dot J \dot q$ over the free joints: a joint held at a
position limit by inverse kinematics (or pushed outward by the
unconstrained solution) gets zero velocity and acceleration, as it has in
the position path. For a redundant robot the motion in the null space of the
task is not set by the task, so it is taken from the returned positions by
finite differences in time. The result is a full `robot_trajectory` that
`robot_traj_check()` can test against velocity and acceleration limits:

```{r}
jt <- robot_traj_cartesian(from, to, duration = 2, n = 101, robot = arm,
                           initial = c(0.3, -0.8), weights = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0))
all(jt$converged)
# Joint velocities map back to the commanded Cartesian velocity.
i <- 30
J <- robot_jacobian(arm, jt$joint$q[i, ])
rbind(commanded = jt$velocity[i, 1:2], achieved = (J %*% jt$joint$qd[i, ])[1:2])
plot(jt$joint, "qd")
```

`derivatives_ok` flags samples where the derivatives do not describe the
path: inverse kinematics failed there, or the path jumps to another
solution branch. Here two serial sliders reach for a point behind the
first slider's lower limit; that slider stays at its limit and the second
one does all the work:

```{r}
sliders <- robot_model(joints = list(
  robot_joint("a", "prismatic", "base", "mid", axis = c(1, 0, 0), limits = c(0, 1)),
  robot_joint("b", "prismatic", "mid", "tip", axis = c(1, 0, 0), limits = c(-2, 2))))
st <- robot_traj_cartesian(robot_pose(), transl(-1, 0, 0), 1, n = 21, robot = sliders,
                           initial = c(0, 0), weights = c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0))
cbind(st$joint$qd[c(6, 11, 16), ], commanded = st$velocity[c(6, 11, 16), 1])
all(st$derivatives_ok)
```
